title: Split Array Largest Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: trying every split combination versus binary search on the max-sum, using a greedy piece-count as the feasibility check.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, split nums into k non-empty CONTIGUOUS subarrays, minimizing the largest sum among these k subarrays. Return that minimized largest sum.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: As the allowed maximum piece sum (a candidate cap) increases, the number of contiguous pieces needed to keep every piece under that cap can only decrease or stay the same. This monotonic relationship between the cap and pieces needed is exactly what "binary search on the answer" exploits.

blocks.title: Analogy: Splitting a Long Rope into the Fewest Pieces Under a Weight Limit
blocks.text: Picture a rope with varying thickness along its length, needing to be cut into pieces so no single piece exceeds a weight limit, using as few cuts as possible. A higher weight limit always needs fewer or equal cuts; binary searching over the candidate weight limit finds the smallest limit that still allows splitting into exactly k pieces.

blocks.caption: A larger candidate max-sum always needs fewer or equal pieces, enabling binary search

blocks.text: Result: 18. Splitting as [7,2,5] (sum 14) and [10,8] (sum 18) gives largest sum 18, the minimum achievable.

Before trying every possible way to split nums into k contiguous pieces, notice that the number of pieces needed to keep every piece's sum under a candidate cap is a monotonically non-increasing function of that cap, letting binary search directly find the minimum feasible cap.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: For a fixed candidate cap, a GREEDY left-to-right scan (accumulate a running sum, starting a new piece whenever adding the next element would exceed the cap) computes the minimum number of pieces needed to respect that cap.

Observation 2: The minimum possible cap is max(nums) (since no single element can be split across pieces), and the maximum useful cap is sum(nums) (everything in one piece).

Observation 3: As the candidate cap increases within this range, the greedy piece count can only decrease or stay the same, a monotonic relationship.

Observation 4: Binary searching over this range, using the greedy piece-count (compared to k) as the feasibility check, converges on the minimum cap for which exactly k or fewer pieces suffice.
This leads to binary searching over candidate max-sums in [max(nums), sum(nums)], computing the greedy piece count at each candidate, and narrowing toward the minimum cap where pieces needed <= k.
Try every way to split nums into exactly k contiguous pieces (via recursion choosing split points), tracking the minimum possible largest piece sum across all valid splits.

items: Recursively try every position to place the next split point, given a remaining number of pieces to form.
For each complete split into exactly k pieces, compute the largest piece sum.
Track and return the minimum such largest sum across all valid splits.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Trying every possible split point combination directly implements the definition, guaranteed correct.
This explores an exponential number of ways to place k-1 split points among n-1 possible positions, far too slow beyond small inputs.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: exponential in the worst case, roughly O(n choose k-1) split combinations explored.
Space: O(n) recursion depth plus O(n) for prefix sums.

Limitation: since the number of pieces needed for a given cap is monotonic, binary search on the candidate cap, using a greedy piece-count check, achieves O(n log(sum(nums))) instead of exploring every split combination.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why exploring every split combination is unnecessary: the actual GOAL is just to find the minimum feasible cap, and a greedy piece-count check at a fixed cap can be computed directly in O(n), without trying every split position.

The binary search reformulation: binary search over candidate caps in [max(nums), sum(nums)]; for each candidate, greedily determine the number of pieces needed (start a new piece whenever adding the next element would exceed the cap).

Why the greedy check is valid: for a FIXED cap, greedily packing as much as possible into each piece before starting a new one always uses the minimum possible number of pieces for that cap (delaying a split as long as possible never increases, and can only decrease, the total pieces needed).

The core idea: binary search directly on the answer (the cap), using an O(n) greedy piece-count as the monotonic feasibility check.

Binary search cap in [max(nums), sum(nums)]. At each step, greedily count pieces needed to keep every piece's sum <= cap; if pieces needed <= k, the cap is feasible (search for a possibly smaller cap); otherwise search for a larger cap.

blocks.caption: Binary search the cap, using a greedy piece-count as the feasibility check

blocks.text: The greedy piece-count function is provably optimal for a fixed cap: packing as many elements as possible into the current piece before starting a new one never uses more pieces than any other valid strategy respecting that cap. Since this piece count is monotonically non-increasing in the cap, the binary search invariant holds: feasible caps (pieces needed <= k) allow searching for a possibly smaller cap, while infeasible caps require searching larger, converging exactly on the minimum achievable largest piece sum.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimize the maximum piece when splitting into exactly k contiguous groups", think: binary search on the max-sum, using a greedy piece-count as the feasibility check.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The exponential split-combination search is infeasible beyond small inputs; binary search with a greedy feasibility check runs in O(n times log(sum(nums))) time and O(1) space.

items: Pattern: binary search on the answer (the max piece sum), using a greedy piece-count as the monotonic feasibility check.
Core Idea: binary search cap in [max(nums), sum(nums)]; greedily count pieces needed to respect the cap; narrow toward the minimum feasible cap.
Time: exponential for trying every split, O(n times log(sum(nums))) for the optimized binary search.
Most Important Observation: the greedy piece count is monotonic in the candidate cap, enabling binary search directly on the answer.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known, frequently reused "binary search on the answer" template problem.
One line memory trick: binary search the cap; greedily count pieces as the feasibility check.
